article.quickAnswer: A mitigation block is an order-block variant in ICT and smart money teaching: after a trend attempt fails to take out its prior extreme, price breaks structure the other way, and the last candle or small group of candles in the failed push is marked as a zone to watch on a return. A rejection block is a wick zone: the span from a candle's body edge to the tip of a long wick at a swing high or low.
takeaways: Both are zones you mark on a chart, defined by candles. They record what happened; they do not prove who traded or why.
A mitigation block is defined by a failed swing plus a structure break. A breaker is its near twin, separated by whether the final swing swept the prior extreme.
A rejection block is defined by a wick: body edge to wick extreme at a swing high or low, usually after a sweep of an old extreme.
Teachers draw both zones in more than one way. Choose one construction, write it down, and keep it.
The explanation traders give (trapped traders exiting, stranded late buyers) is a story. The practical claim is only that these zones sometimes produce reactions, and zones fail regularly.
No independent testing is cited here. Treat both as chart references that need your own tested rules, costs and risk limits.

sections.title: 1. First, What 'Mitigation' Means (and What It Does Not)

blocks.text: Two different things share the word.

rows: Price trades back into a marked zone, so the zone is 'used' or 'mitigated'
'The order block was mitigated on the retest.'
A specific zone defined by a failed swing and a structure break
'The bearish mitigation block formed after the lower high.'

blocks.text: A mitigated order block is not a mitigation block. Keep the words apart and the rest of the topic gets much easier.

Search warning: 'mitigation' also means risk reduction in cybersecurity, and 'ICT' often means information and communications technology. This guide is about the trading concept from Inner Circle Trader (ICT) teaching.
One-minute order-block recap (beginners)

An order block is a candle (or small group) marked at the origin of a strong move, commonly the last opposite-direction candle before it. Traders watch it for a reaction when price returns. A mitigation block and a rejection block are relatives of the order block: one is defined by a failed swing, the other by a wick.

Beginner picture: think of a door that was pushed open. An order block marks where the push started. A mitigation block marks the spot where a push failed before everything turned around. A rejection block marks the spot where something was pushed away, like a long wick poking out and being sent back.
A mitigation block forms in a three-part sequence:

items: A trend attempts to continue. For example, price has been rising and tries to make a higher high.
It fails to take out the prior extreme. Price makes a lower high, staying below the previous swing high.
Structure breaks the other way. Price then breaks below the prior swing low, ideally with displacement.

blocks.text: The zone is the last up-closing candle, or small group of up-closing candles, in the failed rally (bearish case). When price later returns to that zone, traders watch for it to act as resistance. The bullish case mirrors everything: a failed lower low, a higher low, and a break above the prior swing high, with the zone marked on the last down-closing candles.

rows: Lower high (fails to exceed the prior swing high)
Higher low (fails to undercut the prior swing low)
Last up-closing candle(s) in the failed rally
Last down-closing candle(s) in the failed decline

blocks.text: Why is it called 'mitigation'?

The usual explanation: traders who bought into the failed rally are now trapped as structure breaks against them. When price rallies back to their entry area, some sell to escape near break-even, reducing, or 'mitigating', the loss. That exit selling, plus new positioning by trend traders, is said to produce the reaction.

Honest note: that is a plausible story, not something a chart can show. All a chart shows is where candles formed. The practical claim is only that these zones often attract reactions, and they fail often too.

sections.title: 3. How to Identify a Mitigation Block

blocks.text: The sequence matters more than any single candle.

rows: Pick the reference extreme. In an uptrend, the latest swing high; in a downtrend, the latest swing low
Is the swing obvious on the timeframe you trade?
Watch the next push fail. Bearish: a lower high that does not trade above the reference high
If price sweeps beyond the extreme, reclassify as a possible breaker
Confirm the break. Price must break the opposite swing (the pullback low), ideally with displacement
A close beyond the swing, not a wick
Mark the block. The last opposing candle(s) in the failed push, using one consistent drawing rule (full range or body only)
Wait for the return. The zone is traded on a retest, not on formation
Define invalidation. Acceptance (a close) beyond the far side of the zone

blocks.text: Mitigation block worked example (invented prices, bearish)

items: Prior swing low: 100.00. Price rallies to a swing high of 110.00, pulls back to 104.00, then rallies again but stops at 108.50, a lower high.
The last up-closing candles of that failed rally span 107.20 to 108.50. That is the mitigation block.
Price then closes below 104.00 with a large candle (the structure break).
Later, price rallies back to 107.50, inside the block, and prints a rejection candle.
A trader using these conventions places a stop above the block and failed high at 108.80. Risk = 108.80 − 107.50 = 1.30. A target at 103.60 gives reward 3.90, or 3R.
Break-even win rate before costs = 1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%. Spreads, commissions and slippage raise that rate.

blocks.text: All prices are invented to show arithmetic. They are not market data.
The bullish mirror: a failed lower low, a higher low, a break above the prior swing high, the zone on the last down-closing candle(s), and a return from above.
This is the question most learners search. The two zones form around a reversal with a structure break. The deciding test is one question:
Did the final swing sweep beyond the prior extreme before reversing? Yes → a breaker block (the extreme was swept first). No, it fell short → a mitigation block.

Sweeps beyond the prior extreme, then reverses
Trapped traders from a failed push
A failed order block whose role flips, with breakout traders also trapped
Last opposing candle(s) in the failed swing
The broken order block (the last opposite candle before the move that failed)
Liquidity sweep part of the definition?
Same side as the break (a former support becomes resistance, and the reverse)

blocks.text: Why traders care: the sweep version is thought by many to leave more trapped traders, so it is often treated as the stronger setup. That is a view, not a measured result.
Looser usage you will meet: some teachers call any violated order block a breaker. If you read or watch a lesson, check how that teacher defines each term before comparing notes.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: the more tightly you define it, the easier it is to test and the fewer trades you will have.
Propulsion block (related, definitions vary): an order block that interacts with a preceding order block. Some pages describe it differently, so confirm the teacher's version before using the term.
A rejection block is built from a wick, not a candle body.

items: Bearish rejection block: at a swing high that printed a long upper wick, the span from the top of the candle body up to the wick high.
Bullish rejection block: at a swing low that printed a long lower wick, the span from the bottom of the body down to the wick low.

blocks.text: It typically forms after a sweep: price runs above an old high (or below an old low), grabs resting orders, and is sent back, leaving a long wick as the record.

rows: A close beyond the wick extreme
A close beyond the wick extreme

blocks.text: The story told about it: late buyers were filled near the top and stranded; if price returns, those levels may be defended. Again, a story.
Do not confuse it with the vacuum block. In ICT vocabulary a vacuum block is a gap-based idea (an untraded jump), not a wick zone. Community content often mixes the two names.

sections.title: 7. How to Identify a Rejection Block

rows: Find a prominent swing high (or low) with a long wick, ideally one that swept an obvious prior high, session high or equal highs
Measure the wick against the candle's range and recent candles
A minor wick on a minor swing is just candle shape
Mark the zone: body edge to wick extreme
Use the same rule every time
Wait for price to leave and show a new direction
The zone is traded on return
Plan the entry inside the zone on the revisit, stop beyond the wick extreme
Define failure: a close beyond the wick extreme means the zone is spent

blocks.text: The 50% level of the wick

Many traders mark the midpoint of the wick zone (also called the mean threshold, the same 50% idea as consequent encroachment on a fair value gap). It is used as a second reference: an entry level, or a test of whether price is respecting the zone. It is a convention, not a law.
The wick-size filter

How long must the wick be? There is no standard. Some indicators let you set a minimum share of the candle's range as a setting (one common default is half of the candle). Treat any number as a choice you test, not a rule.
A second method: the three-candle version

Some video lessons describe a three-candle construction: the middle candle carries the long wick, and the candle that returns to test it must not close beyond the wick's 50% level for the block to count. If it closes beyond, the block is discarded. This differs from the wick-zone method above. As summarised from a video lesson, wording and details vary, so check the original teacher's rule before relying on it.
Rejection block worked example (invented prices, bearish)

items: An old high sits at 98.80. A candle spikes to 99.00, then closes at 98.00 after opening at 98.20. Its body top is 98.20.
Rejection block = 98.20 to 99.00. Width 0.80. Midpoint = 98.60.
Price leaves, makes a lower low, then rallies back up.

blocks.text: Which block do I mark? A quick decision guide

items: Is there a long wick at a swing extreme, ideally after a sweep? → consider a rejection block.
Did a push fail short of the prior extreme and then structure break? → a mitigation block.
Did price sweep the extreme first, then reverse and break structure, flipping an old order block? → a breaker block.
Did a strong move start from one clear last opposing candle? → an order block.
Do two of these overlap? → note it, and ask whether the second adds independent information.

blocks.text: All of these are conventions that different teachers and models use. None is a tested edge on its own.

A close beyond the far side of the zone (acceptance)
A close beyond the wick extreme

blocks.text: That table follows from geometry: the deeper the level, the fewer returns reach it. Compare the models under identical stops, targets and costs, and count the orders that never filled.
Arithmetic you can rely on

items: Position size = amount at risk ÷ stop distance. On a 10,000 account risking 1% (100), a stop distance of 1.30 allows about 76 units.

Break-even win rate before costs = 1 ÷ (1 + R). At 2R it is one trade in three (33.3%); at 3R, one in four (25%). Spreads, commissions and slippage raise it, and unfilled orders reduce the number of trades.
A stop order becomes a market order when triggered and can fill away from the stop price.

What a sound indicator should do

items: Use confirmed swings only. A swing needs several bars on each side to be confirmed, so any tool that marks it sooner may repaint.
Use one stated drawing rule (full range or body, single candle or group).
Let you set a wick filter (for rejection blocks) and a minimum zone size.
Track each zone's state: untested, tested, midpoint tested, closed beyond.
Not redraw zones after the fact.

blocks.text: Plain-language logic: bearish mitigation block

find confirmed swing highs and swing lows (N bars on each side)
for each swing high H1 followed by a swing low L1:
    find the next swing high H2 after L1 # the failed push
    if H2 < H1: # fell short, no sweep
        if a later candle closes below L1: # structure break
            block = last up-closing candle(s) before H2 turns down
            record zone (block.low, block.high), state = untested
    if H2 > H1:
        treat as a possible breaker, not a mitigation block
Plain-language logic: bearish rejection block

for each confirmed swing high candle c:
    bodyTop = max(c.open, c.close)
    wick = c.high - bodyTop
    if wick >= minimum wick size (a share of c.range or a multiple of ATR):
        zone = (bodyTop, c.high)
        mid = (bodyTop + c.high) / 2
        state = untested
after each later candle, update the state:
    tested, midpoint tested, or spent if a candle closes above c.high
Look-ahead warning: a swing is only known after the confirming bars close. A chart or backtest that marks the block at the swing candle uses information from the future and gives fake results.
What I found: in the sources I read, none showed an independent test of either pattern, and several said plainly that the order-flow explanation is a story. So this guide makes no performance claims.

Why testing these is hard: both blocks leave many choices open: how many bars define a swing, what counts as an obvious high, which candles to include, how long a wick must be, which entry model to use. Each choice is a chance to fit the rule to past charts without noticing.

blocks.text: A mitigation block is a failed push plus a break. A rejection block is a wick at a refused extreme. Both are simple to draw and easy to over-trust. Learn the definitions, pick one drawing rule, keep the failures in your records, and let tested rules, not stories, decide what you do.

faqs.question: What is a mitigation block?
faqs.answer: A mitigation block is an order-block variant from ICT teaching. A trend push fails to reach its prior extreme, then structure breaks the other way, and the last opposing candle or small group in the failed push is marked as a zone. Traders watch it for a reaction when price returns.

faqs.question: What does mitigation mean in ICT trading?
faqs.answer: Mitigation means price trading back into a marked zone, such as an order block or fair value gap, so the zone is considered used. It is an event, not a pattern. The mitigation block is a separate, specific pattern defined by a failed swing and a structure break.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a mitigation block and a breaker block?
faqs.answer: Both form around a reversal with a structure break. A breaker's final swing sweeps beyond the prior extreme before reversing; a mitigation block's final swing falls short of it. Sweep means breaker, failure means mitigation block. Some teachers use 'breaker' loosely for any violated order block, so check definitions.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a mitigation block and an order block?
faqs.answer: An order block is the last opposing candle before a strong move, marked at the move's origin. A mitigation block is a specialised case defined by a failed swing and the structure break that follows. It is built from opposing candles, but not every order block is a mitigation block.

faqs.question: How do you identify a bearish mitigation block?
faqs.answer: In an uptrend, wait for a push that makes a lower high without exceeding the prior swing high. Then require a break below the prior swing low. Mark the last up-closing candle or small group in the failed push, and treat the zone as a candidate resistance on a return.

faqs.question: How do you identify a bullish mitigation block?
faqs.answer: In a downtrend, wait for a push that makes a higher low without undercutting the prior swing low, then a break above the prior swing high. Mark the last down-closing candle or small group in the failed decline and watch it as candidate support on a return.

faqs.question: Where do you place the stop on a mitigation block trade?
faqs.answer: Common conventions place the stop beyond the far side of the zone or beyond the failed swing extreme, so it is not inside the zone. Zones are areas, not exact lines. Choose one rule before testing, and size the position from the stop distance.

faqs.question: Do mitigation blocks work?
faqs.answer: Nothing cited here shows they have a measured edge. They are chart references that often attract reactions and often fail. Whether a rule built on them is profitable depends on exact definitions, costs and risk control, so test your rules with out-of-sample data before risking money.

faqs.question: What is a rejection block?
faqs.answer: A rejection block is a wick zone in ICT teaching. At a swing high with a long upper wick, the span from the candle body's top to the wick high is marked as a bearish block; the bullish version mirrors it at a swing low. Traders watch it on a return.

faqs.question: How do you mark a rejection block?
faqs.answer: Find a prominent swing extreme with a long wick, ideally after a sweep of an old high or low. Draw the zone from the body edge to the wick extreme, add the 50% midpoint if you use it, and wait for price to leave and return. A close beyond the wick extreme invalidates it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a rejection block and an order block?
faqs.answer: An order block uses the candle at a move's origin, usually the last opposing candle. A rejection block uses the wick at a rejected extreme. One marks where a move launched, the other where a push was sent back, and the wick zone is usually narrower.

faqs.question: Is a rejection block the same as a vacuum block?
faqs.answer: No. In ICT vocabulary a rejection block is a wick span at a refused extreme, while a vacuum block is a gap-based span, an untraded jump. Some community content uses the names interchangeably, so check the author's definition before comparing lessons.

faqs.question: What is the 50% level of a rejection block?
faqs.answer: It is the midpoint of the wick zone, also called the mean threshold. Traders use it as a second reference, either as an entry level or as a test of whether price respects the zone. It is a convention, and price can pass through it.

faqs.question: How big does the wick need to be?
faqs.answer: There is no standard. The wick should be large relative to the candle's range and recent candles, at an obvious swing extreme. Some indicators use a minimum share of the candle range as an adjustable setting. Pick a rule, test it, and do not change it after seeing results.

faqs.question: Should I use a mitigation block or a rejection block?
faqs.answer: They answer different questions. A mitigation block describes a failed push plus a structure break; a rejection block describes a wick at an extreme. Use whichever your written rule calls for. When both appear in the same area, ask whether the second adds independent information.

faqs.question: Do these work on all timeframes and markets?
faqs.answer: The shapes can be marked on any candlestick chart. How a rule performs differs by market, timeframe, session and price feed, and thin markets produce long wicks that mean little. Test each market and timeframe separately instead of assuming results carry over.

faqs.question: Can I use an indicator to find them?
faqs.answer: Yes, but check how it works. Swing-based tools confirm a swing only after several bars, so a tool that marks it earlier may repaint. Check the drawing rule, wick filter and mitigation rule, and compare its marks with your own written definition.

faqs.question: Does a rejection block need a liquidity sweep?
faqs.answer: Many descriptions place rejection blocks at swept highs or lows, and some rule sets require the sweep. The wick-zone definition itself does not. State whether your rule requires one, because that choice changes which wicks you mark.

faqs.question: Are these concepts part of ICT teaching?
faqs.answer: Yes. They come from Inner Circle Trader teaching and are widely used in smart money concepts. Sources do not credit one classical author for the names. You can mark the candles without accepting claims about institutional intent, which a chart cannot show.

faqs.question: How can a beginner practise?
faqs.answer: Mark blocks on past charts using one written rule, freeze the chart at the moment of formation, then reveal later candles and log what happened. Record no-returns, failures and ambiguous cases as well as reactions. Practise in replay or on a demo account first.
